facts.fact: Oxygen enters aquarium water mainly at the surface, so the rate depends on how fast the surface layer is renewed.
In a shallow aquarium a bubble reaches the surface within seconds and transfers little oxygen directly; its main value is the upward flow and surface disturbance it creates.
A filter outlet that ripples the surface and circulates the water usually supplies enough oxygen for a normally stocked tank.
Air stones and sponge filters both create surface bubbles that promote gas exchange, and both need an air pump.
Surface agitation helps the exchange of both oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Water's oxygen capacity falls from 9.09 mg/l at 20 °C to 7.56 mg/l at 30 °C, about 17% less.
In a cited goldfish study, oxygen consumption rose about 2.5 times between 21 and 30 °C.
Guidance cited for warmwater fish: 5.5 mg/l dissolved oxygen as a long-term average and 3 mg/l as the absolute minimum.
Rule of thumb for sizing an air pump: about 100 l/h of air for a 100-litre tank.
Small air pumps draw 2–5 W, medium pumps 4–8 W and large multi-outlet pumps 8–20 W.
Air pumps run continuously but use very little power, in the same range as the smallest nano filters (3–6 W).
Heaters (rated 25–500 W) are the largest power users in most freshwater tanks, far more than air pumps.
Gasping at the surface is a late sign of low oxygen.
Gasping can also be caused by nitrite poisoning, ammonia damage or too much CO2, so test the water as well.
Situations that raise oxygen demand or lower supply include summer heat, heavy stocking or large fish, bacterial blooms or cloudy water, and medication treatments.
Filter bacteria use oxygen day and night; nitrification needs about 4.6 g of oxygen per gram of ammonia-nitrogen.
During blackouts plants respire but do not photosynthesise, so they add to oxygen demand.
When the air pump stops, for example in a power cut, water can siphon back through the airline toward the pump unless a check valve stops it.
Airline tubing that has dried and hardened can loosen at the connections and drip during a power outage.
During a power cut, do nothing to the tank for the first 1–2 hours.
If the power is out for 8 hours or more, run air for 1 hour, then repeat every 8 hours.
For overstocked tanks or fish that are gasping, run oxygen sooner and more often, for example every 4 hours for an overstocked African cichlid tank.
Do not feed during an outage and turn off automatic feeders.
In warm weather, feeding and digestion use up oxygen, so do not feed fish during an outage.
Stirring the water with a whisk can raise oxygen when the water is too warm.
In summer, remove items floating on the surface to improve gas exchange.
Keeping the tank dark during an outage helps because fish use less oxygen at night.
A canister filter can lose oxygen within about 4 to 6 hours; remove the media, rinse it in tank water and put it in the tank so the bacteria survive.
Unplug HOB and canister filters during an outage, and clean them before plugging them back in, so decaying organics are not flushed into the tank.
If ammonia rises above 1 ppm without filtration, change 10 to 30 percent of the water.
For transport, fill heavy-duty bags one-third with water and two-thirds with air (pure oxygen is better); lightly stocked fish should survive at least 36 hours.
After power returns, wait 24 hours before feeding.
After power returns, test ammonia, nitrite and pH, and do water changes if needed until the filter catches up.
Installing a check valve: cut the airline between the air pump and the device, and fit the valve in between.
The end of the check valve with the flapper (a coloured or horizontal bar) faces the air pump; if no air flows, the valve is in backwards and must be flipped.
Mount the check valve outside the tank near the top rim, not in the water.
Cut airline tubing straight and cleanly, with no tears.
To cut noise, put the pump on a sponge or felt pad, avoid glass or thin boards, do not hang it by its tubing, and reduce airflow with a gang valve.
Any air-driven device (sponge filter, ornament, brine shrimp hatchery, CO2 system) needs a check valve unless the pump or CO2 tank sits higher than the tank rim.
Use a check valve whenever the air pump sits below the water line.
Back-siphoning water can damage the pump, flood the floor and, in extreme cases, cause an electrical fire.
A battery-powered air pump with an airstone is the easiest oxygen backup in an outage.
A USB air pump can run from a USB power bank or a laptop.
A battery-backup air pump can run about 20 hours continuously, or 40 hours or more when cycling 15 seconds on and 15 seconds off; lowering airflow extends runtime.
For multi-day outages, a portable gasoline or propane generator is an option.
An alternative power source such as a generator or an extension cord from a working outlet can run the pump/filter and heater.
In CO2-injected planted tanks, daytime aeration drives off CO2; run the air pump only at night, ideally on a timer linked to the lights.
An overly fine diffuser can make an air pump noisier.
Most air pump noise comes from vibration passed to the furniture, not from the diaphragm itself.
GreenAqua says it is wrong to think the bubbles themselves add most of the oxygen in a shallow tank; surface movement does. It also admits it found no measurements at aquarium depth.
GreenAqua notes that in oxygen-supersaturated water aeration removes oxygen rather than adding it.
Vietnamese names used: máy sủi oxy (air pump), van một chiều (check valve), ống dẫn khí (air tubing), quả/đĩa sủi (air stone/diffuser).
Both mains-powered (chạy điện) and rechargeable (tích điện) air pumps are sold in Vietnam; tích điện models are the usual backup for power cuts.
Air pump brands sold in Vietnam include Resun, Atman, Sunsun and Hailea.
In the hot season, water near 30 °C holds about 17% less oxygen than at 20 °C, so extra aeration matters more.
Tropical fish tolerate the high 80s to low 90s °F for a day or more, but prolonged heat lowers dissolved oxygen.
Temperature changes of about 10 percent per hour or two should not endanger fish.
Shrimp tanks are especially sensitive to low oxygen.
Most fish can go about a week without food.
